name: manual_c6a0da
claim: Before applying a fix that uses a mechanism with a known-bad prior lesson (e.g. 'flock'), check whether the new usage is actually the SAME mechanism as the prior failure or just shares a name. lesson_8df4d109ae3a warns against flock(1), the util-linux shell CLI tool (absent on macOS by default); fcntl.flock() is Python's wrapper around the flock(2) syscall, present on both macOS/BSD and Linux, and is a different, safe mechanism. Conflating same-named-but-different mechanisms would cause either a false rejection of a safe fix, or worse, missing a real repeat of a past failure when the names differ but the mechanism is the same.
conditions: flock fcntl memory check name collision mechanism identity before applying known-bad-pattern fix

decisions.notes: 2026-07-11: fixed a genuine unsynchronized-file-write race in orama-system's test_concurrent_coord_pulse_calls_dont_race (3 threads racing raw open/read/write with zero locking despite a comment claiming 'file lock prevents corruption') using fcntl.flock(). User asked me to check PT .agent memory + gbrain for prior flock issues before trusting the fix. Found lesson_8df4d109ae3a, verified it was about a different mechanism (flock(1) CLI, not fcntl.flock() syscall wrapper), confirmed fcntl.flock is safe here, and had already empirically verified the fix with 5/5 passing local runs before this check. Good habit: search memory before applying anything with a name-collision to a documented past failure, but verify mechanism identity, not just name identity, before accepting or rejecting.
